utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom and everybody in Belgrade. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, so much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues Barney Thomas and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Saxon. For the Defence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is today represented by much Daniela Tasic, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls witness Rade Orlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rade Orlic. Good morning, Mr. Orlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Orlic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, can you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not receiving ... I hope that this is going to function from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Once again, sir, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: My name is Rade Orlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I was born in Korenica in Croatia on the 7th of April, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the part of Croatia where Korenica is located, does that region have a particular name?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The region's name is Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is Lika part of another region?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know at the moment. During the war, it was in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Orlic, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you retired now?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was pensioned off on the 30th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Orlic, what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I was an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you an officer in the armed forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the military academy in 1963, and then I completed a command staff academy in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so if my mathematics is correct, you served in the army for 32 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, 32 or 33. You're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where in the former Yugoslavia did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: You mean just before the break-up or generally speaking from the moment I graduated to the moment Yugoslavia broke up? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the three areas of the former Yugoslavia where you were based during your time in the army.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I started serving in Pristina. I was there for a year. In 1964, in the month of September, I was transferred to Skopje, and I stayed there until 1975. From 1975 to 1977, I attended a command staff academy in Belgrade, and after having graduated from the academy, I remained in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a specialty in the army?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. My specialty was intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was your rank when you retired?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you served in the Army of Yugoslavia, did you follow orders from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like a distinction to be made between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Yugoslavia. I would like Mr. Saxon to be more precise in those terms. I believe that the previous question was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was a leading question, but I am very willing to be precise, more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you served in the Yugoslav People's Army, did you follow orders from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after the Yugoslav People's Army became the Army of Yugoslavia, did you follow orders from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you were -- what would have happened to you if you had disobeyed an order?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what would have happened, but it never occurred to me anyway. I would not have been able to be a member of either the JNA or the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is asking from the witness to speculate. The question should have been put in the following way: Were you ever in a situation that an order was issued to you and that you did not carry it out? The question as it was put and it was worded as "what would have happened if you had" calls for speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour. This gentleman served in the military for more than 30 years. He was an officer. He followed -- he followed a particular life in the army. I think he is perfectly competent to answer that question based on his knowledge and state of mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but it is still speculative to the extent that we don't know whether, if he disobeyed an order, those above him would have themselves followed procedure to discipline him or whether they would have decided to favour him and not do anything. However, if you ask the question what the rules were when orders were disobeyed, then he can tell you what the rules were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you served in the Army of Yugoslavia, were there rules that addressed soldiers or officers who did not obey orders?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Of course there were rules. However, I never put myself in a situation to disobey an order issued to me. There were all sorts of disciplinary measures that applied to such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. While you served in the Army of Yugoslavia, could you move from one position to another without the permission of your superiors, from one post to another?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. Every transfer was pursuant to an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness a document. It is part of Exhibit P1683. It has -- it would be document ID page 98 in B/C/S. In English, it would be document ID 0611-4942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Saxon, page 98 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Registrar in Belgrade would like you to repeat that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In B/C/S it would be page 98, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you explain what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This document by which I declare that I'm willing to take on duties in the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, a temporary duty. At my own request, I spent 6 months in Lika. I was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Lika, and I formed a staff there. And says here should I be sent to the Krajina again, please take into account the duty that I performed, and then what follows is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, down below towards the bottom of the document, we see a name, Colonel Vladimir Stojkovic. Who was Colonel Stojkovic, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Stojkovic was the chief of the intelligence department in the 1st Army, of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what relationship --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was still the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall approximately when you submitted this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, there is no date. However, I can see that this was immediately after my return from Lika. I returned on the 13th of February, 1992. I could have issued this statement towards the end of 1992 when the Territorial Defence of Yugoslavia was disbanded. After that, I was transferred to the intelligence department in the 1st Army, and this was sometime in either November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a relationship with Colonel Stojkovic of some kind?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: He was my superior. I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: When I moved to the command of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, why did you -- and when you moved to the command of the 1st Army, at that time did the Yugoslav People's Army still exist, or was it the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the Yugoslav People's Army was transformed into the Army of Yugoslavia. I believe that it was in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Orlic, why did you submit this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I submitted it to demonstrate that if there was a requirement in Krajina, and I believe that the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina had already been established, so in the case, my services were required in the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, I submitted the document to show everybody that they can count on me and that I was willing to go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you returned from Lika, and in the second paragraph of the document it says: "I would like to note that I have spent six months in Lika on my own request."

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you return from Lika?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: At that time -- and I said that I returned on the 13th of March. At that time, the situation in Lika started getting better. UNPROFOR had already arrived in the area sometime in February 1992. Preparations were underway for the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Croatia to the border between Bosnia and Croatia, and I believe that there was no need for me to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you simply get into your car and return to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't do that. I asked my superior who was my superior even before I went to Lika, General Djokic, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence [Realtime transcript read in error] of Serbia. I reported to him, I submitted the situation to him, and I requested his leave for me to return to Belgrade, and he gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, in the third paragraph of this document, you wrote the following: "Should I be sent to the Krajina again, please" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A word was omitted from his answer, page 8, line 95. He said General Djokic who was the commander of Serbia, whereas the witness said that General Djokic was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Serbia. I just wanted the record to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, in the third paragraph of your document, you wrote: "Should I be sent to the Krajina again, please take into account the duty that I performed." Mr. Orlic, what did you mean by this phrase "please take into account"?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was my rank and the duty that would correspond to my rank and my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still want to know, the duty that he performed where?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, I don't know if you heard His Honour's question. In that third paragraph, you wrote: "Should I be sent to the Krajina again, please take into account the duty that I performed." Which duty and where are you referring to in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: In 1991 on the 30th of September, I went to Lika when the new Territorial Defence was being formed that was part of the armed forces of the SFRY. And when I wrote this, I meant that if I were to go to Lika again, I wanted to be deployed to a duty that corresponded to my rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This sentence doesn't speak about something that is going to happen in the future. It is talking about something that happened in the past, sir. I want to know where you performed the duty that you want to be taken into account, and when was that duty performed, in which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the commander of the zone HQ in Lika from October until -- October 1991 until March 1992. That was the establishment rank of colonel, and then I thought that if I were to go to Lika again, I wanted to be deployed to a duty that would correspond to my rank, since it was a zone HQ and the TO was later abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a clarifying question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time between October 1991 and early 1992 when you were the commander of the zone Territorial Defence in Lika, what army -- or which army were you serving with?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, the SFRY as a secondary component.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a minute. Sir, you keep saying that if you were to return to Lika you would want that -- the duty you had performed to be taken into account. This letter is making an offer to serve in the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It doesn't make an offer to serve in Lika. So if you are to be redeployed to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, you could be deployed to any other place including Lika but not necessarily to Lika. How would the job you had performed in Lika be taken account of? You say -- okay. You tell me why if you are offering to be returned to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina you should necessarily be deployed in Lika. You tell me why, based on this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean here. It says if I were to be deployed to Krajina again, kindly keep in mind the duties that I was performing. I did not only refer here to the Lika sector, but any place in the Krajina, but to a duty that would correspond to my rank. I could have been sent to Knin, also, Varazdin, anywhere within the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can remove that document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, if you could turn your mind, please, now to the year 1993. Can you recall, during the first half of 1993, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Until the Territorial Defence of Yugoslavia was disbanded, I was at the TO staff as the chief of the intelligence service until the Territorial Defence was disbanded sometime, I don't know exactly, perhaps November 1992. After the TO was disbanded, the TO of Yugoslavia, I was transferred to the commander of the 1st Army as deputy of the -- as first deputy of the chief of the intelligence sector in that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time while you were working for the 1st Army, were you then -- during 1993, was it the People's Army of Yugoslavia, or was it the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I think that the Yugoslav People's Army transformed into the Army of Yugoslavia in late 1992 or early 1993. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Later in 1993, at some point did you leave your position with the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Later on during the year of 1993, at some point did you leave your position at the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia? Did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In mid-November 1993, I went to the Krajina again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you happen at that time to go to the Krajina? How did that come about? Did you simply leave your post, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I went to visit my friends in the personnel centre and the intelligence administration where I worked before from the place where I was working, and it wasn't that far away. So at one time, I found out at the 40th Personnel Centre that some senior officers were going again to Krajina, and that's when I was told I, too, should go. This was sometime in early November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was it, if you recall, at the 40th Personnel Centre who told you you should go to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: At the time Colonel Lalic was there, and Colonel Medakovic. I think Stevo Medakovic was the one who told me that I needed to go to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this 40th Personnel Centre, do you recall what its function was?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The 40th Personnel Centre's duty was to send officers from the Army of Yugoslavia to the Krajina, to send retired senior officers and to send non-commissioned officers there who were born there and wanted to go to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What about active officers like yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The centre also sent active officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you say you had visited your friends at the 40th Personnel Centre and you were told you, too, needed to go to the Krajina. Did you go to the Krajina on the verbal message that you received when you visited your friends, or did you receive a written order to go to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't receive any kind of written order, but it was on the basis of an oral statement. After that, I went to my superior Colonel Stojkovic in the 1st Army, and I told him, and he agreed that I should go. I don't know how this matter was resolved between them, but I did get permission to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the permission you got was oral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you first heard about this at the 40th Personnel Centre, it was just on the chance that -- on the off chance that you happened to be there and this is what you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it just happened that way. Had I not gone, perhaps they would have called me and told me that. I don't know. But in any case, that's how it happened in my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, why did you discuss this move to the Krajina with your superior officer in the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I had to speak to him. I had to get his permission to go. I couldn't just leave the duty that I was performing and go off of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, can you recall the date at this time in November when you left for the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: We set off on the 16th of November in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Orlic, when you say "we," who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: There were a number of officers who were leaving at that time from the Army of Yugoslavia. There were many retired officers, but mostly there were civilians who were going there to their homes or to see their families. There were about five or six buses leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who arranged the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The 40th centre, I assume, because these were military buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 16th of November, which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that you left for the Krajina on the 16th of November, Mr. Orlic, again, what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And where in the Krajina did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I went to Korenica. Three buses with civilians and a good number of the officers came to Korenica. After that, some went to Knin, some went elsewhere, I don't know where, but I remained in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately how long were you in Korenica during that period in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Until the 31st of December, 1993, mostly in Korenica. From time to time, I would go to Knin as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time, did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. My salary was deposited on my chequing account in Belgrade, and my wife had access to that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, your salary from whom?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know now whether that was via the JNA. During the SFRY, this was paid through the SSNO computing or accounting centre. When Yugoslavia was formed, I don't know if it was still processed through that accounting centre or through the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question was not clear. It was my fault. Did you continue to receive your salary from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. During those two months or month and a half --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. During those two months or month and a half, what did you do while you were in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific duties. I was unassigned. I would go and visit my friends and colleagues at the Lika corps command, and I also visited my friends, my colleagues, and fighters at the forward line of defence towards Gospic Otocac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So your position is you spent your time there visiting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No. They were not visits. They were more tours. These were officers and soldiers who were under my command during the section or zone staff in Lika, so I would go and visit or tour there to see how they were doing, what the billeting was like, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Why did you leave -- at the end of December 1993, why did you leave Korenica?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The winter that year was very cold and tough, and probably during those tours I didn't hurt, but I probably in some way injured my knee. It was very swollen. I had difficulty walking, and then I went to the Knin hospital, and they sent me for home treatment in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in Belgrade, where specifically did you receive medical treatment for your knee?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: After the New Year holiday, I went to the military medical academy and started treatment there. I was put in plaster, which I had for three weeks on my knee. After that, I waited for physical therapy at home, and then after a month, month and a half, or two months I was in physical therapy at the military medical centre, the VMA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This military medical centre that you refer to, was it part of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The military medical academy, I don't know if it's a part of the army. I don't know if it's under the General Staff authority or the Ministry of Defence authority, but in any event, it's a military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And after you received that physical therapy in early 1994, did you return to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No. I went back to my prior post at the 1st Army Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And just moving back to something you told us a moment ago at page 16 of the transcript, you explained that when you were in Korenica for those six weeks, you would go and visit the officers and soldiers who had been under your command previously in Lika to see how they were doing and the billeting and so forth. What did you do with the information that you received from those officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't collect any information at that time. I simply went to see their living conditions, the billeting. In view of the fact that it was winter, I wanted to just see what their state of health was, primarily the conditions of accommodation, but I did not really gather any data, and I did not send that on to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to get a little more clarity here on this point. Sir, when you were in Korenica during that period, where was your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have one. I was not deployed anywhere. I would go to the corps command or to these corps units just to see how my friends and acquaintances were doing. I didn't have any specific task or assignment. I didn't have an office. I was staying in my own house because I was born in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you have -- you didn't have any superior you were reporting to you while you were working for those six weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I didn't have a duty, a specific duty to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, when you came to Korenica, you didn't even go to report to anybody within the command structure of the army to say, Here am I, I've been transferred here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reported to the corps command that I had arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Lika Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did they say to you? They didn't give you any instructions as to where you are supposed to be deployed, or, rather, let me say, what did he say to you in this sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that I was not assigned to the corps command, that I would probably be deployed in Knin, but no one called me from Knin, and they knew that I was there, that I had arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, after you received medical treatment in the military hospital in Belgrade, when you then went to the 1st Army, was it again on some oral instruction, oral order by somebody, or how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to the 1st Army because from that post I was sent to Krajina, so it was quite logical that I would come back to my home unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But when you come back to your home unit, don't you come back on some order? You received an oral order to go to the Krajina. Do you just abandon your position in the Krajina and come back, or do you get an order to come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came back from the Krajina because of treatment at the military medical academy. When the treatment there was completed, I went to the 1st Army Command again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my point precisely. You are in Belgrade not on transfer; you are on Belgrade from medical attention. So you are still posted in the Krajina. On what basis do you then transfer yourself from the duties in Krajina to the duties in the 1st Army? You told us at the beginning of your testimony that you just don't change positions without an order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you thinking of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the time when you went to the 1st Army after you received medical treatment in the military hospital. I thought you said that was in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I came back for medical treatment, when the medical treatment was finished, I went once again to the 1st Army command. I reported to my superior. I told him what the situation was, that I was not given an establishment post, that I was not assigned anywhere when I went to the Krajina, to any kind of duty, and this is why I came back to the 1st Army Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that in fact when you left the Krajina to come back now, it was without an order, oral or written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I left the Krajina I reported to the commander of the Main Staff in Krajina. That was General Novakovic. At the time, he was the commander of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I told him what my medical situation was, and he agreed that I should go back. And then when I completed my treatment, I reported to the 1st Army command to see what would happen then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You reported to Novakovic about your medical condition, and he agreed that you go to Belgrade for medical treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is, is it your evidence that you transferred from the Krajina army to the 1st Army without an order of transfer? I'm not talking about an order or permission to go for medical treatment. Is that your evidence, you didn't have this order, oral or written, that you should go back to the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Novakovic when he agreed for me to go for treatment did not tell me that after treatment I had to return to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. My question to you is, you went -- you left the Army of the Krajina and went to the 40th Personnel without an order to do so. Is that your evidence? I just want to know that that is your evidence. I'm not saying it was right or wrong or not right to do so. I'm just wanting to know, did you have an order? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that what you wanted to say was something else; however, it was recorded on line 21 he left Krajina and returned to the 40th centre, and he said left Krajina and returned to the 1st Army, as far as I could understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is what I wanted to be sure of and clarify. As far as I could understand his testimony, after his return to Krajina and treatment at the VMA military academy, he didn't go to the 40th centre. He went back to the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Sir, [Microphone not activated] -- I just want to know, it's a very simple question, you can answer it by saying yes or no. When you left the Krajina, the Army of the Republic of Krajina, to go and rejoin the 1st Army, you had no order, whether oral or written, to do so, or did you? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the oral order to return from Krajina for treatment, this is what I received from General Novakovic. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, sir. I'm not talking about treatment, sir. I'm talking about joining the army, the 1st Army. You had no order to go and join the 1st Army, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but that was my unit from which I had left to go to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you had been ordered to go to the Army of Republic of Krajina; isn't it so? You told us that. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I didn't hear an answer from the witness, but I will proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I saw the witness nod his head to Your Honours's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask him what he meant by nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you mean when you nodded your head, Mr. Orlic, a moment ago to His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This meant that I returned to the command of the 1st Army, and I really don't know who should have issued me an order to go back to the command of the 1st Army. I was deployed in Krajina. When I left, I did not have any establishment duty, and it was only logical for me to return to the command of the 1st Army. I did the logical thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orlic, just so that our record is clear, a few moments ago in response to a question from Judge Moloto, you explained how when you went to the Krajina in November 1993, you reported to the corps command of the Lika Corps. And just so that our record is clear, to which army did the Like Corps belong to?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The Lika Corps belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orlic, I'd like you to please turn your mind to the year 1994, and particularly the month of May 1994. In the first part of May 1994, where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I was posted in the 1st Army. I was the assistant or deputy chief of the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point during May 1994, did your situation change?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: You mean while I was in the command of the 1st Army, or generally speaking in the month of May of that year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask my question perhaps more specifically. At some point in May 1994, did you leave the 1st Army and go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of May, maybe around the 20th May, Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic arrived from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. At the time, he was the chief of the intelligence centre. That was on the intelligence department of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. He informed me that General Celeketic who at the time was the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina wanted a word with me, and this had to do with my return to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Orlic, if we could just go a little bit more slowly, please. You mentioned that General Celeketic at that time was the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. Prior to going to the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, do you know where General Celeketic served?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Before becoming the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, he was in Western Slavonia. I suppose, I'm not sure, but I believe that he had arrived from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know which army he belonged to prior to serving with the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, and later on he was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did this Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic explain to you why General Celeketic wanted a word with you?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He told me that that was about my joining the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did he tell you -- did he tell you in what capacity you might join that Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: There was a vacancy. The chief of the intelligence department in the command of the Main Staff of the army was the vacant position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Earlier, you mentioned that Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic arrived from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. At that time in May 1994, where was the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina located?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So did Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic speak to you at your post in the 1st Army in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And -- and were you able to leave your post at that time and go to speak with General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I had to ask my superiors permission to go to Knin. I did ask him. At that time, it was Colonel Pavlovic. He was the chief of the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you receive permission to go to Knin and speak with General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I received permission, and I left around 25th of May. I went to talk to General Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in summary, can you describe the meeting that you had with General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Knin, in General Celeketic's office we talked about a possibility for me joining the Main Staff and taking over the duty of the chief of the intelligence department there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was it just you and General Celeketic at this meeting, or were there others present?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Smiljanic was also there. At the time, he was the chief of the security department. I don't remember and I'm not sure whether General Loncar was also there. I don't think so, but I'm not sure. General Loncar was the Chief of Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time what response, if any, did you give to General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I agreed that I would come to Knin and assume the duty. However, before that I had to consult with my superiors, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you're referring to your superiors, your superiors where now?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to my superior in the command of the 1st Army, Colonel Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And upon consulting with Colonel Pavlovic, what did he tell you, or what was the outcome of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Knin, I told him my -- I relayed to him our conversation in Knin, and he agreed that I could go back to Krajina and that I could take over the duty in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that we understand now, if General Celeketic was the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina and you were serving in the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time, what authority did General Celeketic have to offer you that post in the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the offer of a post, he did not have any authority. He only had the need to fill the post. He knew that I hailed from the area, that I hailed from Lika. He also knew that I was an educated intelligence officer. He probably had all that in mind, and that's why he offered me the position. Whether he talked to anybody else, the personnel centre or somebody else about my transfer, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you recall, then, how --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I see the time. Would this be a moment to take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's convenient to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, shortly before the break, you explained how after you returned from your meeting with General Celeketic, you spoke to your superior in the 1st Army, Colonel Pavlovic, and that he agreed that you could go to Knin to take up this position in the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Can you recall, or do you know, who or whom actually made the arrangements for you to go to Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know who it was. In legal terms, I don't know who organised my departure. However, I returned to Knin with Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you returned to Knin, do you recall if you received -- while you were in Belgrade, do you recall if you received any telephone calls about this matter?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you given any written order of transfer to Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you receive an oral order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received an oral consent of my superior, Colonel Pavlovic. He approved with my departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following up on Judge Moloto's question, did you receive any other verbal communication from within the Army of Yugoslavia about you going to Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall when you went to Knin to take up this post in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I arrived on the 1st of June. I believe that it was on the 1st of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you went -- when you left your position in the VJ 1st Army and went to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina on that day, did you join the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I joined on a permanent basis, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, were you expected to remain with the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina until the end of your career?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. What were your duties while you worked in Knin in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of the intelligence department of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in that capacity, did you exchange information with other entities?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, within the army or outside of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I mean outside of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I exchanged intelligence with the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska and intelligence administration of the Army of Yugoslavia from time to time as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you describe a little bit. What kind of information would you exchange?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: That was intelligence about the situation, the movements of the Croatian army units in Bosnia and the Army of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during your duties in Knin in 1994, did you have occasion to request information from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I had such occasion. If something was not clear to me as regarded the movements of the units of the aforementioned armies, and if I did not have any concrete intelligence research from the intelligence centre or from other organs of the Army of Republika Srpska, I would request information from the intelligence administration or the intelligence organs of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, because I had asked -- the question was whether you had requested information from the Army of Yugoslavia, but in the English translation at the end of your last response --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration of the Army of Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, thank you very much. And when you made such requests, did you receive the kinds of information that you requested from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the Army of Republika Srpska? Did you have occasion to request information from the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Most often I requested information from the corps of the Army Republika Srpska. Its command was in Drvar. I had personal contacts with some of the members of the intelligence centre under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic. From time to time, I would also request information from the Main Staff or whatever it was called from the intelligence organ of the Army of Republika Srpska there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would your request for information from the Army of Republika Srpska be fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Usually that was the case. That was always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see you looking at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, just one little point I want to get cleared. Sir, after this transfer, now, after you took up position with the Main Staff in Knin, which army paid your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My salary was paid into my current account in Belgrade. My wife had the power of attorney, and I received a supplement from the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, and that was to cover the cost of my accommodation and living in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was which army paid your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the autumn of 1994, Mr. Orlic, did you become aware of the activities of a unit known as the 5th Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We monitored the activities and movements of those units, as we did of all the other units of the Army of Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the activities of the 5th Corps have any effect on your reporting during the autumn of 1994, frequency of your reporting?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in view of the fact that the activities, i.e., combat activities started sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you're referring to combat activities starting sometime in September, combat activities between whom?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: On the one hand we had the 5th Corps, and on -- and the Army of Republika Srpska; and on the other hand, some of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so how often, then, would you -- were you reporting to the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Republika Srpska about this combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Not often. I really can't say now how many times a month that was, but it wasn't very frequent, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Even during September and October of 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: It was more frequent then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: But I really couldn't say how frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orlic, while you served in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina during 1994, did you ever receive orders from the Army of Yugoslavia, either verbal or written?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, I never received any oral or written order from the Army of Yugoslavia. All the orders I received came from the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, while you served in the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina in 1994, if you had received an order from the Army of Yugoslavia to return to Belgrade, would you have obeyed the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is based on the same question Mr. Saxon put at the beginning and which I objected to as speculation. The Prosecutor asked whether he received; he said no, and now he is asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was a professional officer. He knows what his state of mind is and was at the time as well as his experience and what his duties were, so this is not asking for speculation. In addition, Your Honour, there is precedent here for such kinds of questions. I'd respectfully direct the Chamber's attention to the proceedings against Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski, case number IT-04-82-T; the transcript of proceedings from the 25th of May, 2007; pages 1443 to 1445 of the transcript, where counsel asked a police officer from Macedonia: "In 2001, would you have carried out an operation without an order from your superior?" And that question was permitted. And it's the Prosecution's submission that we are in the same situation here today. We are really going to the state of mind of the witness. I'm not asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] just very briefly, Your Honours. I think that what Mr. Saxon has now given us as an example we cannot assess. We don't know if there were any objections and in which context it was asked and granted. What I'm concerned about, Your Honours, is that questions like this can open up Pandora's box of questions of what would happen if. I can put scores of such questions regarding to status, and if we are talking about the state of consciousness and mind of the witness at the time, and what he says about that now is something else. So the answers that the witness could give us now about his state of mind ten years ago would not have the adequate weight and would not be of assistance to the Chamber in determining the truth. It boils down to a situation of classic speculation, and then I'm afraid that if we get into these questions and such a practice is permitted now, the Trial Chamber will make it possible for many assumptions to be brought in. This case is important because of statutory rights and census, so this is the gist of what the court has to deal with and not based on something that the witness assumes would happen if something would happen. Now we have checked the transcript from this Boskoski trial, and we see there was no objection to a question put in this way. So we are just informing the Chamber about that particular matter in relation to the question that Mr. Saxon is putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, questions about a state of mind that a witness may have had or had years ago are very common in this Tribunal. Were you afraid at that time; this is -- you know, this is the case where we have a person who lived a particular kind of life with a particular kind of responsibility, and he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the question "were you afraid at that time" is not a speculative question. It's a fact question. Through your experience, through your life, at that time were you afraid? If he was afraid: Yes, I was afraid at that time. He is telling you something that did happen. He is not speculating on what would happen if something happened. Now, the question as you formulated is classically speculative. And the fact that another Chamber in this Tribunal allowed the question, particularly under circumstances where there was no objection, does not mean that this Trial Chamber must do the same. And in fact, you are not even referring to -- I don't know whether that's a Trial Chamber or an Appeals Chamber question. I would suspect it's a Trial Chamber given the fact that it's a trial thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this Chamber is not bound by the decision of that Chamber. That decision may just be a passive decision, but that is also not a decision. It's a just a question being asked, no objection, and the witness answers, without necessarily the Chamber exercising its mind on the question because it was not raised an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I'm withdrawing my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, how long did you remain within the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina in Knin in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I stayed until the 31st of December, 1994. I came back to Belgrade on the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you leave your position with the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This is one of the reasons why, amongst other things, I went to the Krajina. At the time, my mother was in Korenica over the summer, and she came back in -- she came back to Belgrade in September, and this was one of the reasons, since she was quite sick. At the time she was 91 years old, and this is mostly why I asked to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you receive permission? When you say "go back," did you receive permission to go back?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked about it for awhile with my superior, General Loncar. The conversation took over a month, and the request for my retirement I submitted I think in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you refer to a request for retirement, retirement from who or from what?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Retirement from the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify this in the cross-examination, but I think that it would be proper in relation to the response on page 36, line 7, when the witness said to my superior General Loncar. Who was General Loncar? Where was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to clarify that, sir? That's not an objection. He is just suggesting to you on how to ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to do that if counsel asks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said you spoke to General Loncar. Who was he at that -- and what position did General Loncar have in the autumn of 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: General Loncar was the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika -- of Srpska Krajina. He was my superior while I was in the Krajina. I could not return from the Krajina without his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, how would you describe your relationship with the Army of Yugoslavia while you served in the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in any relationship with them. I was subordinated to the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is part of Exhibit P1683. This is document ID in English, 0611-4947; and in B/C/S, it would be page 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see this document in front of you, Mr. Orlic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You see your name at the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document and my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's titled "Cessation of Professional Service Due to Early Retirement, Own Request," sent to the 1st Army Command. The 1st Army Command, was that part of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The command of the 1st Army was part of the Army of Yugoslavia. However, I submitted my request via the personnel section of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. I submitted my request to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: It was not directly sent to the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you take a look at the third paragraph, please, sentence beginning with the word "Currently ..." Can you read that sentence out loud to us, please?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: "Currently, I'm temporarily assigned to the 40th Personnel Centre of the Army of Yugoslavia, and I'm in the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of" -- "of the Army of the Serbian Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is, was the 40th Personnel Centre of the Army of Yugoslavia essentially the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No, the 40th Personnel Centre was not part of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness from the same exhibit -- we can take that exhibit away, please. Can we show the witness from the same exhibit, in English it would be doc ID 0611-4931; and in B/C/S, 087, at the end. And if we could in the English version move down just a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Orlic?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was what?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: A document granting or recognising my work or stay in the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says under the word "decision," it says that Colonel Rade Orlic is granted the right to -- actually, in the first line it refers to Colonel Rade Orlic, son of Sava, from Military Post 4001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know what Military Post 4001 was?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know which military post that is, if it's the military post of the centre or a military post of the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. In the second line, it says: "... is granted the right to years of double pensionable service for the period from 8 October 1994 to 31 December 1994." Do you know why you had the right to double pensionable service for that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This was a decision of the government of Yugoslavia for all members who were in the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina to recognise their wartime service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we remove that document, please, and show the witness, again, from P1683, document ID 0611-4935-091. This is the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel is asked to state the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The B/C/S page I believe is 91, 9-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, we see this is an order of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslavia army dated 31 December 1994. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document on the cessation of professional military service. Actually, it's my retirement document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why didn't you retire from the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina or in the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I don't know why not. I assume that because I was sent from the Army of Yugoslavia to the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, it was logical for me to ask for retirement from the Army of the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we didn't hear due to interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlic, the interpreters may have missed the very last part of your response. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: I said that I was sent by the Army of Yugoslavia, even though that was at my own request and in agreement with General Celeketic. But still, I went to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from the Army of Yugoslavia, and then I thought it would be logical for me to request retirement from a professional service from the Army of Yugoslavia because as far as I know, the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina did not in any way participate in any retirement of professional officers or personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall the date when you officially retired?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: When I retired?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: This was the 30th or the 31st of March, 1995. That's when my active military service stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you happen to sign something on that date?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed the order on the cessation of professional military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where did you sign that order?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: At the 1st Army Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that's in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Orlic. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orlic, good morning. My name is Novak Lukic, and I'm going to be asking you certain questions on behalf of Mr. Perisic's Defence. Before we start, I have a warning both for you and for myself to wait after my question before starting your answer to allow the interpreters to interpret into English. I'll also do the same thing after your answer. Everything has to be adequately interpreted, you know.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that if nothing else, at least during the last years of your active service, you were actively involved in intelligence activities; am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber and for us to be able to grasp the essence of the intelligence service, I'm going to tell you, and you tell me whether you agree with me, that in general terms, military and intelligence service deals with a collection and processing of intelligence on the enemy military force and on the threats to the army that you are a member of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I say that intelligence activity is a planned and targeted activity by appropriate military and other organs and units to collect and process intelligence on a potential (in peacetime) and real enemy during combat -- to avoid any confusion, I've been reading from a textbook. This is a textbook definition.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The goal of any intelligence activity is to discovery the economic and military power, the intention of the enemy as a whole, and the intentions of each and every of its units in particular.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. In other words, everything that may have an effect on the development, equipment, and engagement of the military force of any other country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you have already testified today, for a while you worked as an intelligence organ, i.e., the assistant chief of the intelligence for the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of the tasks and objectives of your activity, the activity you were involved in, was to provide your commander, the commander of the 1st Army with information and intelligence which was important for the proper functioning of the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were a member of the intelligence organ of the 1st Army, you received and exchanged information about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because that situation particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia was of some interest for the security and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were particularly interested in information about the regions which were in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia close to the border of the zone of responsibility of the 1st Army; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the forces across the Drina and the forces in East Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me, Mr. Orlic, that in military and strategic terms, it is in the best interest of an army when it comes to intelligence and completely customary to exchange information with other allied militaries?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is customary, and such intelligence is gathered and obtained in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What ways? Could you just tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: By and large, we are talking about the activities in the regions around the border undertaken by the friendly army; second of all, when it comes to the Army of Yugoslavia, it is regular exchange of intelligence and information between military attaches, mixed reconnaissance, troop reconnaissance of the units in contact, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we have obtained this picture, now that we are a bit more clear about what the intelligence organ did, I've always had a problem distinguishing between the security and intelligence organs, but I believe that we are now clear and that the Trial Chamber will understand what you are talking about. Now we are going to move on to the answers you provided to Mr. Saxon's questions, and let's try and focus and analyse your stay and your status in Krajina. In factual terms, as we have heard from you, you were in Krajina three times, and every time you were engaged in your professional officer's duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first time you were there was at the time when the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed before the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established. Back then, you were part of the system of the armed forces of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on. You were saying?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: The new Territorial Defence was then established in the territories of Serbian Krajina which were inhabited predominantly by the Serbian population. The previous Territorial Defence which had comprised the entire Republic of Croatia broke up, and the Territorial Defence was another form of armed forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, and the system had to be re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time as an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, you were first a member of the Territorial Defence of Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then the newly established Territorial Defence of Krajina became part of the system of the armed forces of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was at the time and the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina was not established yet, and you said that you actually returned when that army started being established.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: It was still the time of Territorial Defence, which was part of the armed forces of the SFRY. After that when the Army of Yugoslavia withdrew from the area, what remained were territorial units of the Republika Srpska Krajina, which later on became the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the first time you went there, you had sought consent from your superior in the Yugoslav People's Army or in Serbia. In any case, it was part of a command chain of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes. My superior at the time was General Djokic who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Serbia. I asked his approval to go to Krajina in order to establish the zone staff, which was part of the new Territorial Defence of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'm going to have a few questions about your second departure to Krajina. As you have described for us, the second time you went there was during the period when the legal and factual conditions had changed. The period in question is between 16 November and 31st December, 1993. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was a time when you were a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, a member of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the time when the Serbian Army of Krajina had been established and existed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was already in place. The Serbian Army of Krajina already existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness the Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina. In order to speed my examination along, I prepared some things. Just a moment, if everybody can bear with me, please. This is 65 ter 6367, page 11 in B/C/S and page 4 in the English version of the document. Can we scroll down a little. I need Article 1 of the army law. Yes, that's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read Article 1: "The Serb Army of Krajina, hereinafter the army, is an armed force which defends the sovereignty, territory, and independence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Right?

utterances.speaker: RADE ORLIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
